title: 7 Best Chainsaws in 2026: Gas and Battery Saws by Job
keywords: what is the best chainsaw brand
what are the best chainsaws for home use?
description: The Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss is the best chainsaw for firewood; the EGO CS1800 is the #1 battery saw for storm cleanup. 7 saws ranked, with sizing and safety.
dek: The Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss is the best chainsaw for firewood; the EGO CS1800 is the #1 battery saw for storm cleanup.
intro: The best chainsaw for firewood and storm work is the Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss, a 50.2cc gas saw sold and serviced by local dealers, and the best battery chainsaw is the EGO Power+ CS1800, an 18-inch, 56-volt saw that handles most suburban storm cleanup with no fuel. Between them, they cover what most homeowners actually cut.

A chainsaw is the most dangerous tool most people own and one of the most useful after a storm. That is why the right saw is usually smaller than the one that looks impressive in the store. This guide ranks seven gas and battery chainsaws by job, then answers the questions buyers type: gas or battery, which brand, what size, how to avoid kickback, what gear to buy, when to call a pro and how to keep the saw running.
quickAnswer: Buy the Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss or Husqvarna 450 Rancher for firewood and storm work, and the Echo CS-590 only if you cut big hardwood every year. For gas-free storm cleanup, buy the EGO CS1800; for light limbing, the Ryobi 40V 14-inch or DeWalt 20V MAX 12-inch. Milwaukee M18 owners should look at the M18 FUEL 16-inch. Buy chaps and a helmet with any of them.

blocks.p: Buy the smallest saw that handles your usual wood, not the biggest tree on the property. A lighter saw is easier to control, and control matters more for safety than raw power.

For storm cleanup in a suburb, the EGO CS1800 is the best chainsaw for most people. For firewood, buy the Stihl MS 271 or Husqvarna 450 Rancher from a dealer, and step up to the Echo CS-590 only if you cut big hardwood every year.

These rankings rely on manufacturer specifications such as engine displacement or battery voltage, recommended bar lengths, weight, chain brake and other safety features, and warranty terms, plus the service network behind each brand and recurring themes in owner feedback. Each saw is matched to a realistic homeowner job. None were put through cutting trials for this guide.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss

blocks.p: The MS 271 Farm Boss is the saw rural owners most often tell a neighbor to buy for heating with wood and cleaning up after storms. Its 50.2cc two-stroke engine is sold with bars in roughly the 16 to 20-inch range, enough for firewood rounds and moderate blowdowns without wearing you out by lunch. Stihl fits a chain brake, a side-access chain tensioner on many configurations, and a long-life air filtration system that stretches the time between filter cleanings. The biggest advantage is how it is sold. Stihl goes through local dealers who assemble the saw, walk you through safe starting and chain tension, and handle repairs, which is worth real money for a first-time owner. Like every mid-size gas saw, it is loud, it vibrates, and it needs mixed fuel and regular care. It is far more saw than light pruning calls for, but for firewood and storm work it is a durable, proven choice.

**Pros:** 50.2cc engine handles firewood and storm cleanup; 16 to 20-inch bar options; local dealer setup and service; long-life air filter. **Cons:** Loud with noticeable vibration; needs mixed fuel and regular maintenance; too much saw for light pruning.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Stihl+MS+271+Farm+Boss&tag=sktiger-20)

The 450 Rancher is the Farm Boss's main rival and is often priced a little lower. It also uses a 50.2cc engine and usually ships with an 18 or 20-inch bar, and you can buy it from dealers or big-box stores. Husqvarna equips it with an inertia-activated chain brake, a starting system designed to reduce pull effort, an air injection system that spins heavy debris out before it reaches the filter, and anti-vibration dampening. It handles firewood, felling small to moderate trees and storm cleanup. Where you buy matters. A dealer sets it up and services it; a big-box purchase often saves money but may leave you assembling the bar and adjusting chain tension yourself, which you need to learn properly before the first cut. Like any gas saw, it is loud and heavy for pruning, and it should be stored with stabilized or ethanol-free fuel so the carburetor stays clean.

**Pros:** 50.2cc engine with 18 to 20-inch bars; often priced below rivals; air injection pre-cleaning; sold at dealers and big retailers. **Cons:** Big-box purchases may need self-setup; loud and heavy for pruning; needs fuel care in storage.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Husqvarna+450+Rancher+chainsaw&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Bigger Wood: Echo CS-590 Timber Wolf

blocks.p: Echo's CS-590 Timber Wolf steps up to a 59.8cc engine with bar options around 18 to 24 inches, which gives it more pull in big hardwood rounds and large blowdowns than the 50cc saws above. Echo is known for long consumer warranties, and the Timber Wolf has been a long-running favorite with owners who cut a lot of firewood but do not want to pay professional saw prices. That extra power comes with weight, and you feel it over a long day. It is also more saw than most suburban owners need, and a bigger saw with a longer bar demands more skill to control safely. For someone who heats with wood and processes several cords a year, or who regularly faces large trees on rural land, it delivers a lot of power for the money. Read the warranty terms before you buy, because coverage typically depends on using Echo's own two-stroke oil.

**Pros:** 59.8cc engine for big hardwood and blowdowns; bars up to about 24 inches; strong consumer warranty reputation; excellent power for the price. **Cons:** Heavy for long sessions; more saw than most homeowners need; demands experience to control.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Echo+CS-590+Timber+Wolf&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Battery Chainsaw: EGO Power+ CS1800 56V

blocks.p: EGO's CS1800 is an 18-inch battery saw on EGO's 56-volt platform with a brushless motor, and for homeowner work it comes about as close to a mid-size gas saw as battery saws get. It starts with a trigger squeeze, sits silent between cuts, needs no fuel mix and runs far quieter than gas. EGO includes a chain brake and an automatic chain oiler, and many versions have tool-free chain tensioning. For storm cleanup, cutting downed limbs and occasional firewood, it is a genuinely capable tool. Runtime depends on battery size and the wood: a large pack covers a cleanup session, but several cords of hardwood will mean multiple batteries and charging breaks, and dense hardwood bogs it more than a gas saw. It is heavy with a big pack installed. If you already own EGO batteries for a mower or [leaf blower](/best-cordless-leaf-blower/), it is the easiest way to a full-size saw without gas.

**Pros:** 18-inch bar on a 56V brushless platform; instant start, quiet idle, no fuel; chain brake and auto oiler; shares EGO batteries. **Cons:** Runtime limits big firewood jobs; slower than gas in large hardwood; heavy with a large battery.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=EGO+Power%2B+CS1800+chainsaw&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Milwaukee Owners: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 16-Inch Chainsaw

blocks.p: Milwaukee's M18 FUEL 16-inch saw is one of the most capable chainsaws on a tool battery platform, aimed at contractors, arborists and serious DIYers who already run M18 batteries. Paired with a high-output M18 pack, it has the power for storm cleanup, limbing and moderate cutting, and it is ready the instant you pull the trigger. Milwaukee fits a chain brake and a metal bucking spike, and some versions offer tool-free tensioning. Cost is the sticking point. It is expensive as a bare tool and more so as a kit, and it performs best on Milwaukee's larger, pricier batteries; small compact packs run it only briefly. Runtime is also shorter than a tank of gas. For an M18 owner who needs a saw a few times a season, it is a strong choice. For someone starting with no batteries, the cost of high-output packs makes it a hard sell next to the EGO or a gas saw.

**Pros:** Strong power on a pro tool battery platform; instant start and quiet idle; metal bucking spike and chain brake; fits existing M18 kits. **Cons:** Expensive, especially with large batteries; needs high-output packs to perform; shorter runtime than gas.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Milwaukee+M18+FUEL+16+inch+chainsaw&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Compact Battery: Ryobi 40V HP 14-Inch Compact Chainsaw

blocks.p: Ryobi's 40-volt HP 14-inch saw is a lighter, more affordable battery saw built for what most suburban owners actually cut: downed limbs, overgrown shrubs, small trees and storm debris. The brushless motor and 14-inch bar are a good match, and the compact size is easier to control than a full-size saw for someone who only picks one up a few times a year. A chain brake and automatic oiler are included. It is not a firewood saw for big hardwood rounds, it slows in thick wood, and the shorter bar limits the log diameter you can cut in one pass. Kits are reasonably priced, and the 40-volt battery also runs Ryobi's mowers, trimmers and blowers, so the pack keeps working through the season. If your saw use is a handful of weekends tidying the yard, this is plenty of saw and far less intimidating than a gas model, which makes it a sensible first chainsaw.

**Pros:** Light and easy to control; brushless motor with 14-inch bar; affordable kits; battery runs Ryobi 40V yard tools. **Cons:** Not for large firewood rounds; slows in thick hardwood; shorter bar limits log size.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ryobi+40V+HP+14+inch+chainsaw&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Small Saw for Limbing: DeWalt 20V MAX XR 12-Inch Compact Chainsaw

blocks.p: DeWalt's 20V MAX XR 12-inch saw is a compact rear-handle battery chainsaw for limbing, pruning and cutting small branches. It runs on the same 20V MAX batteries as DeWalt drills and drivers, which keeps the cost down for anyone already on the platform, and its brushless motor and short bar keep it light and easy to steer. Tool-free chain tensioning, a chain brake and an automatic oiler come standard. Its sweet spot is light work: stripping branches off a downed tree, cutting brush, clearing a fence line, or turning small limbs into kindling. It is not meant for felling or bucking large logs, and forcing it into big wood is slow and hard on the battery. Runtime depends on the pack you fit, so a larger 20V MAX battery helps on longer jobs. For a DeWalt owner who needs a saw a few times a year around the yard, it is an easy addition to the tool shelf.

**Pros:** Light, compact and easy to control; runs on common 20V MAX batteries; tool-free tensioning; brushless motor. **Cons:** 12-inch bar limits it to small wood; not for felling or big logs; runtime depends on battery size.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DeWalt+20V+MAX+XR+12+inch+chainsaw&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Gas or Battery: Which Chainsaw Is Best for Home Use?

blocks.p: The decision comes down to how much wood you cut and how big it is.

A good 40 to 56-volt battery saw now handles storm cleanup, limbing and occasional firewood with no fuel, no pull cord and silence between cuts. Battery saws start instantly, need far less maintenance and are lighter in compact sizes. Their limits are runtime and sustained power: big oak rounds drain a pack quickly, and a full day of cutting needs several batteries and a place to charge.

Gas saws run as long as you have fuel and bar oil, and a 50cc saw has more sustained power in big wood than most battery saws. They win for all-day firewood sessions and remote spots far from an outlet.

blocks.p: Corded saws are a budget option for light work near an outlet, but the cord is a hazard around a moving chain. Most owners are better served by a battery saw on a platform they already use for a [weed eater](/best-weed-eater/) or [leaf blower](/best-cordless-leaf-blower/).

Heat with wood or own wooded acreage: buy a dealer-supported gas saw and learn to maintain it. Cut a few times a year after storms: a battery saw is safer to start, easier to store and more pleasant to use.

sections.h: What Is the Best Chainsaw Brand?

blocks.p: There is no single best chainsaw brand for everyone; the right one depends on whether you want gas with dealer service or a battery saw that shares packs with tools you own.

Stihl, Husqvarna and Echo dominate homeowner gas saws. Stihl sells through local dealers who assemble, explain and service the saw. Husqvarna sells through dealers and big retailers. Echo is known for long consumer warranties, usually tied to using its own two-stroke oil.

EGO, Milwaukee, DeWalt and Ryobi lead battery saws. EGO and Ryobi are outdoor-focused platforms with mowers, trimmers and blowers. Milwaukee and DeWalt come from the trade tool side and make the most sense if you already own their batteries. Battery saws are sold mostly through large retailers, with service handled through the maker's warranty.

Ryobi's 40V saws are cheaper and suit occasional yard work; Milwaukee's M18 FUEL saws are built for contractors and perform best on large, expensive packs. If you own neither, compare complete kits. If you own one platform, the saw that fits your batteries is usually the better value. Our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) comparison and [Ryobi tools review](/ryobi-tools-review/) cover those platforms in more depth.

blocks.h3: What matters more than the badge

blocks.p: A nearby dealer or service shop, parts availability and a chain brake that works matter more than brand loyalty. Buy where you can get help.

sections.h: What Size Chainsaw Do You Need?

blocks.p: Match the bar to the wood you normally cut. A bar a couple of inches longer than your typical log diameter lets you cut through in one pass.

Longer is not better for most owners. A long bar adds weight out front, makes the saw harder to control and enlarges the kickback zone at the nose. Most people cutting firewood and storm debris are well served by 16 or 18 inches.

Gas saws of roughly 35 to 45cc are light homeowner saws for limbing and small trees. The 50 to 55cc class is the sweet spot for firewood and storm cleanup with an 18 or 20-inch bar. Saws of 60cc and up are for big hardwood and heavy use, with more weight and vibration.

Battery saws are rated by voltage and motor type. Brushless motors are more efficient, and higher-voltage platforms such as 56 or 80 volts, or high-output packs on 18 to 20-volt systems, pull longer bars faster.
Compare weights with bar, chain and fuel or battery fitted; bare powerhead weights on the box understate what you will carry. Fatigue makes mistakes more likely.

blocks.h3: Match the bar to the saw

blocks.p: Use only bar lengths the maker lists for your saw, with a chain of the correct pitch, gauge and drive-link count. If a tree is more than about twice your bar length in diameter, or it leans, is hung up, or is near a building or power line, call a certified arborist.

sections.h: How Do You Avoid Chainsaw Kickback?

blocks.p: Kickback is the sudden, violent upward and backward motion of the bar toward you. It happens when the upper quarter of the bar's nose, the kickback zone, touches wood or another object while the chain is moving, or when wood pinches the chain. It happens faster than anyone can react.

Every consumer saw should have a chain brake triggered by the front hand guard and, on most saws, by inertia during kickback. Test it before each use as the manual directs; if the chain does not stop instantly, the saw is out of service. Also look for a throttle lockout, a chain catcher and a rear right-hand guard. Battery saws add an electronic brake and trigger lockout. Most homeowner saws ship with low-kickback chain, and US gas saws are designed to meet ANSI B175.1, which includes kickback performance; electric saws are evaluated under UL standards. Replace chain with the low-kickback type specified for your saw.

Keep the bar nose clear of other logs, branches and the ground. Start cuts at full throttle, hold the saw with both hands and thumbs wrapped, keep your left arm straight, and stand to the side of the cutting path. Never cut above shoulder height, never run a saw one-handed, and never use one on a ladder. Leave plunge and bore cuts to trained users. Support logs so the cut opens; on a log supported at both ends, cut partway from the top and finish from below.
A dull chain forces you to push, which leads to loss of control, and a loose chain can derail.

sections.h: What Safety Gear Do You Need to Run a Chainsaw?

blocks.p: Budget for protective gear as part of the saw.

head: Gear
Why it matters
What to look for
rows: Fibers jam the chain on leg contact
Gas saws damage hearing over time

blocks.p: Chainsaw chaps or pants contain long fibers that are pulled into the sprocket and stop the chain if it touches your leg. Size them to cover from the waist to a couple of inches above the ankle. No garment guarantees protection, but they are the single most important item.
A forestry helmet system combines a hard hat, face screen and earmuffs. Add safety glasses under the screen. Battery saws are quieter, but hearing protection is still sensible over a long session.
Wear gloves for grip and boots with protective toes. Skip loose clothing and jewelry. Keep a first aid kit that can control serious bleeding nearby, and avoid cutting alone.

sections.h: When Should You Call a Pro Instead of Cutting Yourself?

blocks.p: Most homeowner saw injuries happen during cleanup, but the worst ones happen during felling.

blocks.h3: Leave these trees to an arborist

blocks.p: Do not fell a tree that leans toward a structure, has dead or broken limbs overhead, is near power lines, is larger than your training covers, or is hung up in another tree. Call a certified arborist or tree service.

Trees and saplings bent under tension, called spring poles, can snap with great force when cut. Root plates can tip back upright when a trunk is freed. Broken limbs hanging overhead can fall without warning. Assume every downed line is energized, stay well clear of anything touching or near one, and report it to the utility. OSHA generally requires workers without line-clearance training to keep at least 10 feet from overhead lines; treat that as an absolute minimum.

In open ground, check the lean, clear brush, and plan two escape routes about 45 degrees back from the fall line. Keep everyone at least two tree lengths away. Cut a proper notch and back cut that leaves a hinge, and walk away along your escape route as the tree starts to fall.

A [hookaroon](/best-hookaroon-reviews/) moves rounds without bending over the saw, and a [log splitter](/best-log-splitter/) handles splitting. For clearing brush on acreage, a [compact tractor](/best-compact-tractor/) does the heavy hauling.

sections.h: How Do You Maintain a Chainsaw?

blocks.p: A sharp chain throws large chips; a dull one makes fine dust and needs pushing. Touch up the cutters with a round file of the correct diameter every couple of tanks or charges, or whenever you see dust. Any contact with dirt or rock dulls the chain instantly. A file guide holds the angle, and depth gauges need occasional lowering. Many dealers sharpen chains inexpensively, and a spare chain lets you swap in the field.
With the saw off, the chain should sit snug against the underside of the bar yet pull around by gloved hand. Check before each use and often during the first hour with a new chain, which stretches.

Use bar and chain oil, not motor oil, and keep the reservoir full. Flip the bar periodically, clean the groove and oil holes, and file burrs off the rails. Replace the drive sprocket after two or three chains.

Most modern two-stroke saws use a 50 to 1 gas and oil mix; follow your manual and use a quality two-stroke oil. Use fresh fuel with stabilizer or ethanol-free premix, and never straight gas. Refuel with the engine off and cool, and move several feet away before starting. For storage, run the tank dry or stabilize it and clean the air filter. Store battery packs indoors, partly charged. Always fit the bar scabbard.

Beyond the saw, budget for a full set of protective gear, files, bar oil and a spare chain. For firewood, pair a dealer-supported gas saw with a good splitter. If the job is bigger or riskier than your skill, a professional is the cheapest option.

mistakes: A big saw with a long bar feels capable in the store, but it is heavier, harder to control and has a larger kickback zone. Most homeowners cut wood well within reach of a 16 or 18-inch bar. Buy the smallest saw that handles your typical wood; control beats raw power for safety.

Many chainsaw leg injuries happen in a split second when the saw kicks back or slips while limbing. Chaps that meet a recognized standard can stop a running chain, and a helmet with a face screen guards against falling limbs and chips. Buy the gear with the saw, not after a close call.
Cutting with the nose of the bar

The upper quarter of the bar tip is the kickback zone. If it touches a log, branch or the ground while the chain is moving, the saw can be thrown back toward your face. Watch the tip at all times, keep it clear, and leave bore cuts to people trained to make them.
Cutting trees under tension without training

Storm-bent trees and limbs pinned under other trees store huge energy and can spring back violently when cut, and root plates can flip upright. If you cannot read the tension clearly, or there are power lines anywhere near, stop and call a certified arborist or tree service.
Running a dull or loose chain

A dull chain forces you to push the saw, which brings fatigue and loss of control, and a loose chain can come off the bar. Sharpen as soon as the saw makes fine dust instead of chips, and check tension before every use and often during a new chain's first hour.
bottomLine: For storm cleanup and occasional cutting in a suburb, the EGO CS1800 is the best chainsaw for most owners, with the Ryobi 40V 14-inch and DeWalt 20V MAX 12-inch for lighter limbing. For firewood, the Stihl MS 271 Farm Boss and Husqvarna 450 Rancher are the proven mid-size gas choices, and the Echo CS-590 Timber Wolf suits people who cut big hardwood. Whatever you buy, get chaps, a helmet with a face screen, and eye and ear protection with it, test the chain brake before every use, keep the bar tip clear, and leave leaning, hung-up, large or near-line trees to a certified arborist.

faqs.q: What is the best chainsaw for home use?
faqs.a: For most homeowners, the EGO Power+ CS1800 is the best chainsaw for home use: an 18-inch, 56-volt brushless saw that handles storm cleanup and occasional firewood with no fuel. For lighter limbing, the Ryobi 40V HP 14-inch is easier to control. If you cut several cords of firewood a year, buy a 50cc gas saw like the Stihl MS 271.

faqs.q: What is the best chainsaw brand?
faqs.a: Stihl, Husqvarna and Echo are the leading gas chainsaw brands, and EGO, Milwaukee, DeWalt and Ryobi lead battery saws. Stihl stands out for local dealer setup and service, Echo for consumer warranties, and EGO for battery saws that come close to mid-size gas. The best brand for you is the one with nearby service or batteries you already own.

faqs.q: Are battery chainsaws strong enough for firewood?
faqs.a: Good 56 to 80-volt battery saws and high-output pro platform saws can cut firewood, especially softer woods and moderate log diameters. The limit is runtime: a big hardwood pile drains batteries quickly, so you need several packs and charging time. For several cords of hardwood a year, a 50 to 60cc gas saw remains more practical.

faqs.q: What size chainsaw does a homeowner need?
faqs.a: For pruning and small limbs, a 12 to 14-inch battery saw is enough. For storm cleanup and occasional firewood, a 16 to 18-inch battery saw or a 40 to 50cc gas saw is the sweet spot. Bars of 20 inches and up make sense only for big hardwood and experienced users. Buy the smallest saw that handles your typical wood.

faqs.q: What is the best chainsaw for the money?
faqs.a: The Husqvarna 450 Rancher is the best gas chainsaw for the money, with a 50.2cc engine and 18 to 20-inch bars often priced below rivals. Among battery saws, the Ryobi 40V HP 14-inch gives the most for the price for suburban limbing. If you already own batteries from a platform, the bare-tool saw for those packs is usually the best value.

faqs.q: How do I keep a chainsaw from kicking back?
faqs.a: Keep the upper quarter of the bar tip away from logs, branches and the ground. Hold the saw firmly with both hands and thumbs wrapped, keep your left arm straight, start cuts at full speed and stand to the side of the cutting line. Never cut above shoulder height, keep the chain sharp, use low-kickback chain and test the chain brake before every use.

faqs.q: What fuel mix does a chainsaw use?
faqs.a: Most modern two-stroke chainsaws use a 50 to 1 mix of gasoline and two-stroke oil, but always follow the ratio in your owner's manual. Use a quality oil made for air-cooled two-stroke engines and fresh fuel with stabilizer, or ethanol-free premix. Never run straight gas, which can ruin the engine within minutes. Some warranties require the brand's own oil.
